input: whats that scheduler with a bunch of priority queues that moves jobs around based on how they behave?
expected_output: That is the Multi-Level Feedback Queue (MLFQ). It has multiple levels of queues and uses feedback to determine the priority of a given job: it pays attention to how jobs behave over time and treats them accordingly.

evidence.quote: We have described a scheduling approach known as the Multi-Level Feedback Queue (MLFQ).
it has multiple levels of queues, and uses feedback to determine the priority of a given job. History is its guide: pay attention to how jobs behave over time and treat them accordingly.

input: why do brand new processes get dropped into the top queue instead of the bottom one?
expected_output: The scheduler can't tell whether a new job will be short or long, so it first assumes the job might be short and gives it high priority. If it really is short it runs quickly and finishes. If not, it slowly moves down the queues and proves itself to be a long-running, batch-like process.

evidence.quote: because it doesn’t know whether a job will be a short job or a long-running job, it first assumes it might be a short job, thus giving the job high priority.

If it actually is a short job, it will run quickly and complete; if it is not a short job, it will slowly move down the queues, and thus soon prove itself to be a long-running more batch-like process.

input: why does the os every so often shove every single job back up to the first queue? what does that even fix
expected_output: It fixes two problems. First, jobs can't starve: sitting in the top queue means a job shares the CPU with other high-priority jobs in round-robin fashion, so it eventually gets service. Second, if a CPU-bound job turns interactive, the scheduler treats it properly once it has been moved up.

evidence.quote: First, processes are guaranteed not to starve: by sitting in the top queue, a job will share the CPU

with other high-priority jobs in a round-robin fashion, and thus eventually receive service. Second, if a CPU-bound job has become interactive, the scheduler treats it properly once it has received the priority boost.

input: why do the upper queues get tiny slices of cpu time while the bottom ones get way bigger ones?
expected_output: The high-priority queues hold interactive jobs, so quickly alternating between them makes sense and they get short slices. The low-priority queues hold long-running CPU-bound jobs, so longer slices work well there.

evidence.quote: The high-priority queues are usually given short time slices; they are comprised of interactive jobs, after all, and thus quickly alternating between them makes sense
The low-priority queues, in contrast, contain long-running jobs that are CPU-bound; hence, longer time slices work well

input: why would a cpu heavy job never get to run? doesnt every process get a turn eventually
expected_output: Not in the basic version. If there are too many interactive jobs, together they can consume all the CPU time, so the long-running jobs never receive any CPU time and starve.

evidence.quote: First, there is the problem of starvation: if there are “too many” interactive jobs in the system, they will combine to consume all CPU time, and thus long-running jobs will never receive any CPU time (they starve).

input: How is the original way of demoting a job different from the later single rule, and what does the change stop a process from doing?
expected_output: Originally there were two rules: Rule 4a demoted a job one queue only if it used up an entire time slice while running, and Rule 4b kept a job at the same priority level if it gave up the CPU before the time slice was up. The later single Rule 4 demotes a job once it uses up its time allotment at a level, regardless of how many times it gave up the CPU. This stops a process from gaming the scheduler by issuing an I/O just before its time slice ends to keep its priority and dominate CPU time; whatever its I/O behavior, it slowly moves down the queues and cannot gain an unfair share of the CPU.

evidence.quote: Rule 4b: If a job gives up the CPU before the time slice is up, it stays at the same priority level.
Rule 4: Once a job uses up its time allotment at a given level (regardless of how many times it has given up the CPU), its priority is reduced (i.e., it moves down one queue).
With such protections in place, regardless of the I/O behavior of the process, it slowly moves down the queues, and thus cannot gain an unfair share of the CPU.
Rule 4a: If a job uses up an entire time slice while running, its priority is reduced (i.e., it moves down one queue).
Without any protection from gaming, a process can issue an I/O just before a time slice ends and thus dominate CPU time.

input: why cant the os just use shortest job first or round robin, what's wrong with each one?
expected_output: Shortest-job-first style algorithms are good for turnaround time, but they need to know how long a job will run and the OS generally doesn't know that. Round Robin reduces response time but is terrible for turnaround time. That is why a scheduler is needed that works without knowing job lengths in advance.

evidence.quote: it would like to optimize turnaround time, which, as we saw in the previous note, is done by running shorter jobs first; unfortunately, the OS doesn’t generally know how long a job will run for, exactly the knowledge that algorithms like SJF (or STCF) require.
unfortunately, algorithms like Round Robin reduce response time but are terrible for turnaround time.
How can we design a scheduler that both minimizes response time for interactive jobs while also minimizing turnaround time without a priori knowledge of job length?

input: say jobs P and Q sit in the top queue and R is in a lower one, and none of them ever block for io. what runs over the first four time slices?
expected_output: P and Q have the same priority, so they run in round-robin: P, Q, P, Q. R is on a lower queue, and the job with higher priority is the one chosen to run, so R doesn't get any of those four slices.

evidence.quote: a job with higher priority (i.e., a job on a higher queue) is chosen to run.
Of course, more than one job may be on a given queue, and thus have the same priority. In this case, we will just use round-robin scheduling among those jobs.

dropped: Saying the jobs never block for I/O brings in demotion (Rule 4a/Rule 4): P and Q each use a full slice and drop a level, so the result over four slices depends on which lower queue R is in and on the allotment, both unspecified. If R is one level down, it shares RR with P and Q by slice 3, so 'P, Q, P, Q' is not the single correct answer. The question would need rewriting, not just the answer.

input: 4 queues with 10ms slices, job never does io. how long until it hits the bottom queue?
expected_output: The job enters at the highest priority, the topmost queue. Each time it uses up an entire time slice its priority is reduced by one queue. Going from the top of 4 queues to the bottom takes 3 demotions, each after a full 10 ms slice, so about 30 ms of running.

evidence.quote: When a job enters the system, it is placed at the highest priority (the topmost queue).
If a job uses up an entire time slice while running, its priority is reduced (i.e., it moves down one queue).

input: what does the unix nice command actually do to scheduling, does it force my program to run first?
expected_output: No, it only nudges things. Using nice you can increase or decrease a job's priority somewhat, and thus raise or lower its chances of running at any given time. It is an example of advice: the OS need not pay attention to it, but may take it into account to make a better decision.

evidence.quote: by using the command-line utility nice you can increase or decrease the priority of a job (somewhat) and thus increase or decrease its chances of running at any given time.
We often call such hints advice, as the OS need not necessarily pay attention to it, but rather might take the advice into account in order to make a better decision.

input: mlfq needs you to tell it how long a job runs first right?
expected_output: No. MLFQ doesn't demand advance knowledge of what a job is like. Instead it observes the job's execution and prioritizes it accordingly.

evidence.quote: instead of demanding a priori knowledge of the nature of a job, it observes the execution of a job and prioritizes it accordingly.

input: in mlfq a job that gives up the cpu early to wait on keyboard gets demoted right?
expected_output: No, the opposite. If an interactive job does a lot of I/O it relinquishes the CPU before its time slice is complete, and the scheduler doesn't want to penalize it, so it simply keeps the job at the same level.

evidence.quote: if an interactive job, for example, is doing a lot of I/O (say by waiting for user input from the keyboard or mouse), it will relinquish the CPU before its time slice is complete; in such case, we don’t wish to penalize the job and thus simply keep it at the same level.

input: how can a program game mlfq to keep hogging the cpu?
expected_output: With the early rules, before its time slice is over the program issues an I/O operation to some file it doesn't care about, which gives up the CPU and lets it stay in the same queue. Done right, for example running for 99% of a time slice first, it could nearly monopolize the CPU.

evidence.quote: before the time slice is over, issue an I/O operation (to some file you don’t care about) and thus relinquish the CPU; doing so allows you to remain in the same queue
When done right (e.g., by running for 99% of a time slice before relinquishing the CPU), a job could nearly monopolize the CPU.

input: what goes wrong if the gap between those all-jobs-to-the-top resets is too long, or too short?
expected_output: If the time period is set too high, long-running jobs could starve. If it is set too low, interactive jobs may not get a proper share of the CPU.

evidence.quote: If it is set too high, long-running jobs could starve; too low, and interactive jobs may not get a proper share of the CPU.
